prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Bottle, And, Any

outputs.L1:
“Bottle gatherer, what do you hope to gain from collecting the remnants of other people’s merrymaking, beyond the few cents you will accrue?”

“I will enjoy the echo of their celebration. Besides, the giant snake-head of the bottle bank is at least a block away. I am helping them.”

“And does that bring you pleasure in these days of random mass shootings in bars and music venues?”

“Any bottle that holds drops of wine and not drops of blood pleases me.”

“Do you believe in God, my friend?”

“I am not your friend, good sir, though I wish you well. And I will need at least a year to answer your question.”

“Very well, then—tell me, do you distinguish between green, brown, and colorless bottles?”

“No more than I distinguish between the skin colors or hair colors of our citizens.”

“May I help you, without recompense, bring the bottles to the great metal snake?”

“Ah, kind sir, I thank you, but some journeys are best taken alone.”
outputs.L2:
“Collector of bottles, what do you expect to get from retrieving the leftovers of other people’s revelry, apart from the few coins you will earn?”

“I take pleasure in the lingering trace of their festivities. Also, the bottle bank, with its enormous snake-like metal head, is at least a block from here. I’m doing them a favor.”

“And in an age of unpredictable mass shootings in bars and concert halls, does that bring you any joy?”

“A bottle that still holds a little wine and not a single drop of blood is something I’m glad to find.”

“Do you have faith in God, my good man?”

“I am not your friend, sir, though I wish you no harm. As for your question, I would need no less than a year to give you an answer.”

“Very well. Then tell me this: do you sort green, brown, and clear bottles from one another?”

“No more than I sort people by the color of their skin or the shade of their hair.”

“May I assist you, without payment, in carrying the bottles to the great metal serpent?”

“Dear sir, I’m grateful, but certain paths are best walked by oneself.”
outputs.L3:
The bottle gatherer moves through the streets collecting discarded bottles, doing so partly for the small reward they bring, but not for money alone. Each bottle seems to hold the faint remains of someone else’s celebration: a birthday, a reunion, a shared meal, an evening of laughter. In gathering them, the gatherer savors these traces of joy, as though the happiness that once surrounded the bottles still lingers in their glass.

The work also feels useful. By collecting the bottles, the gatherer saves others the trouble of carrying them all the way to the distant bottle bank. What might seem like a humble or unnoticed task becomes, in the gatherer’s eyes, a quiet service to the community. Each bottle picked up is one less burden for someone else, one small act of order restored to the street.

There is comfort, too, in the kind of bottles the gatherer finds. Bottles that still smell faintly of wine suggest festivity, companionship, and warmth. They are far easier to accept than bottles associated with anger, violence, or harm. The gatherer prefers the evidence of celebration to the evidence of suffering, finding reassurance in the idea that these objects once belonged to moments of pleasure rather than pain.

The gatherer also refuses to make distinctions between bottles based on color. Green, brown, clear—such differences seem unimportant. To the gatherer, judging bottles by their outward appearance is as foolish as judging people by superficial traits. What matters is not the shade of the glass, but the shared purpose and history each bottle carries.

At times, others offer to help with the work, perhaps out of kindness or pity. The gatherer always refuses politely. This is not because help is unwelcome in itself, but because the journey has a personal meaning. Some paths, the gatherer believes, must be walked alone. The solitude is part of the task, giving space for reflection, dignity, and a quiet connection with the lives briefly glimpsed through the bottles left behind.
outputs.L4:
At dusk, when the square was almost empty and the first lamps had begun to shine on the wet stones, a man moved slowly between the benches with a sack over his shoulder. He stooped often. From beneath tables, beside tree trunks, and near the mouths of overflowing bins, he gathered bottles: green wine bottles, brown beer bottles, clear little bottles that had held sweet drinks or cheap spirits. Each one he lifted with care, as if it were not refuse but evidence.

A stranger, who had been watching him from the steps of the fountain, finally spoke.

“Why do you do that?”

The bottle gatherer looked up. He was neither young nor old in any obvious way. His coat was patched, but clean; his beard was gray at the chin; his eyes were mild and alert.

“Because they are here,” he said.

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the beginning of one.”

The stranger came closer. “Do you sell them?”

“When I can.”

“So it is money.”

“It is partly money.”

“Then say so plainly. You collect bottles because you are poor.”

The gatherer smiled. “I am poor enough to notice what others throw away. But poverty is not the whole reason a man bends down.”

“What other reason is there?”

The gatherer took a bottle from the grass and held it up to the light. “This was made from sand, fire, labor, time, transport, wages, quarrels, machines, hands. Someone filled it. Someone bought it. Someone drank from it and forgot it. If I leave it here, it may break under a child’s foot. It may be swept with dirt into a cart and buried where nothing becomes useful. If I take it, it may become again what it was, or something like it.”

“That sounds like service.”

“It may be.”

“To whom?”

“To the street, perhaps. To whoever might have stepped on the glass. To the men who melt it down. To myself, because I eat from it. To the world, if the world accepts small courtesies.”

The stranger laughed softly. “You speak like a priest of bottles.”

“No. Priests usually stand higher than what they bless. I bend lower.”

The stranger studied him. “Do you take pleasure in this?”

“In some parts.”

“In garbage?”

“In order,” said the gatherer. “In finding what was lost. In the clink of glass when it is not breaking. In carrying away what would otherwise lie about accusing everyone.”

“Accusing?”

“Yes. Every discarded thing says, ‘Someone did not care what became of me.’ A square full of such things becomes a sermon no one wants to hear.”

The stranger looked around. The benches were marked with scratches; paper cups rolled in the wind; a smashed bottle glittered near the curb like a small patch of ice.

“And the pleasure?” he asked. “You mentioned pleasure.”

The gatherer set his sack down. “There is sometimes a fragrance left. Wine, beer, lemonade, anise, plum brandy. A ghost of festivity.”

“You smell them?”

“Sometimes.”

“That is pitiful.”

“Is it? I do not drink what remains. I do not steal from the feast. I only meet, after the guests have gone, the harmless trace of their happiness.”

“Other people celebrate, and you collect the remains.”

“Yes.”

“Does that not make you bitter?”

“It might, if I believed their joy had been taken from me. But joy is not bread. If another man eats, I may be hungry. If another man laughs, I need not be poorer.”

The stranger frowned. “That is easy to say.”

“It is difficult to live. But it is still true.”

A tram passed at the far end of the square, throwing yellow light over the pavement. For a moment the bottles in the sack gleamed through the opening like captured stars.

The stranger said, “You are too gentle. The world is not gentle.”

“No.”

“Men strike one another for less than the value of your sack.”

“Yes.”

“They despise weakness.”

“Yes.”

“They fear strangers, hate neighbors, praise equality, and step over anyone lying in the road.”

“Yes.”

“And you think collecting bottles answers any of that?”

“No,” said the gatherer. “It does not answer it. It refuses to imitate it.”

The stranger was silent.

The gatherer continued, “There is violence in waste. Not the violence of fists, perhaps, but of indifference. A thing is used and cast aside. A place is shared and fouled. A worker’s labor is treated as nothing. The future is asked to swallow what the present did not trouble to mend. I cannot stop men from hating each other. I cannot make the proud humble or the frightened brave. But I can pick up this bottle.”

He did so.

The stranger watched him drop it into the sack. “You speak of morals as if they can be kept in small acts.”

“Where else are they kept?”

“In laws. In churches. In revolutions.”

The gatherer nodded. “Also in how a man behaves when no one applauds.”

“You believe in God?”

The gatherer tied the sack loosely and sat on the edge of the fountain. “Some days I believe in God. Some days I believe only that belief has visited mankind and left behind duties. It is enough, on doubtful evenings, to behave as if the world were not merely a heap.”

“That is faith?”

“It may be the poor man’s kind.”

“To act as if meaning exists?”

“To act so that meaning has a place to arrive.”

The stranger considered this. “But if there is no God?”

“Then no angel has been offended by my collecting bottles.”

“And if there is?”

“Then perhaps He will recognize the work. Or perhaps He will ask why I did so little. I cannot know.”

“You are humble.”

“I am tired,” said the gatherer. “People often mistake one for the other.”

The stranger smiled despite himself. Then he said, “What about equality? You said you collect the bottles of those who feast. They sit at tables; you bend under them. Are you equal to them?”

The gatherer looked at the café terraces, where chairs had been stacked and waiters were counting money. “In hunger? No. In comfort? No. In the eyes of officials? Usually not. In death? Certainly. In dignity? Only if I do not surrender it.”

“And how does one keep dignity while rummaging through bins?”

“By knowing what one is doing and why. A man may lose dignity at a banquet if he flatters a fool for profit. Another may keep it in a gutter if he serves some clean purpose.”

“You make yourself sound free.”

“I am not entirely free. No poor man is. But neither am I entirely owned by the opinions of those who pass me.”

The stranger glanced away. “I passed you twice before I spoke.”

“I noticed.”

“And what did you think?”

“That you had a question.”

“Not that I despised you?”

“Perhaps you did. But contempt is often only curiosity before it has learned manners.”

The stranger laughed again, this time more openly.

The gatherer rose and lifted the sack. “You have more questions?”

“One more. Are you lonely?”

The answer did not come at once. The square had grown darker, and with darkness came a strange intimacy: the fountain murmuring to itself, the lamps trembling in puddles, distant voices thinning into alleys.

“Yes,” said the gatherer. “Often.”

“Then why not seek company instead of bottles?”

“I do. Sometimes the bottles lead me to people. A waiter gives me soup. A child asks why glass is green. A drunk tells me the story of his ruined love. A widow saves jars for me and calls it an arrangement, though I think she likes to see someone knock. But solitude is not always cured by company.”

“No?”

“No. Some solitude belongs to being human. Some belongs to being poor. Some belongs to seeing too clearly what others prefer to ignore. One must learn which kind is speaking.”

“And which speaks tonight?”

The gatherer looked into his sack. “The ordinary kind.”

“What is that?”

“The kind that says: continue.”

The stranger folded his arms against the cold. “You find meaning in very little.”

“I find little meanings,” said the gatherer. “Large ones have caused much trouble. Men kill each other for large meanings. They burn cities to purify mankind. They build prisons in the name of perfect equality. They murder for flags, doctrines, gods, markets, histories. A bottle asks less. It says only: do not leave me broken in the road.”

“That is enough?”

“For tonight.”

The stranger bent down and picked up a bottle lying near the fountain. He held it awkwardly, as though embarrassed by its emptiness.

“This one?”

The gatherer accepted it with a nod. “Yes. That one too.”

Their hands touched briefly. The stranger seemed surprised by the warmth of the other man’s palm.

“Will you be paid for all these?” he asked.

“Not much.”

“But something.”

“Something.”

“And tomorrow?”

“More bottles.”

“And after that?”

“More streets.”

“That sounds endless.”

“It is,” said the gatherer. “But so is sweeping, teaching, forgiving, nursing, planting, listening, burying the dead, raising children, beginning again after folly. Only destructive things dream of finishing everything.”

The stranger repeated quietly, “Only destructive things dream of finishing everything.”

The gatherer looked at him with approval. “You remember well.”

“I am trying to understand.”

“That is already a form of gathering.”

“What do I gather?”

“Fragments. Questions. Perhaps yourself.”

The stranger gave the faintest bow, unsure whether he was being mocked or blessed.

The bottle gatherer shouldered his sack and began to cross the square. The glass sounded softly with each step, not like coins, not like chains, but like many small bells muffled in cloth. At the corner he paused and turned back.

“Do not think too highly of me,” he called. “I am only collecting bottles.”

The stranger answered, “And do not think too little of that.”

The gatherer smiled, then disappeared into the narrow street where the lamps were fewer.

Left alone by the fountain, the stranger looked at the ground differently. The square had not been transformed. It was still dirty, still cold, still bordered by houses whose windows held separate lives. Fear had not left the city. Inequality had not been repaired. No doctrine had been defeated. No heavenly voice had spoken.

Yet something had shifted. A discarded bottle near the curb no longer seemed merely an object. It was a small test, almost laughably modest, of whether the world must remain as careless as it was found.

After a moment, the stranger picked it up.
outputs.L5:
**Bottle, And, Any**

A bottle can hold many things: water, juice, a message, or even a memory. And sometimes, the simplest object can become important when we need it most. Any bottle, whether made of glass or plastic, can be reused, recycled, or transformed into something new. By taking care of small everyday items like a bottle, we can make better choices for the environment and for the future.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short, philosophical dialogue between a person collecting empty bottles after a night of revelry and a passerby who questions their motives, touching on violence, faith, equality, and solitude.
counterfactuals.output:
**Passerby:** Why gather the bottles? The feast is over. Let the street keep its glitter.

**Collector:** By morning, glitter becomes glass in someone’s foot.

**Passerby:** So you serve the careless?

**Collector:** I serve the barefoot.

**Passerby:** And what of those who broke them? Their singing turned to smashing. There was blood near the fountain.

**Collector:** Violence is often celebration that has lost its memory.

**Passerby:** You speak like a priest.

**Collector:** No. A priest asks heaven to forgive the broken. I ask the earth to hold still while I pick it up.

**Passerby:** Then you have no faith?

**Collector:** I have faith in small acts. A hand, a bag, the next bottle. What else has ever mended the world?

**Passerby:** Justice, perhaps. Equality.

**Collector:** Equality begins here: the rich drink, the poor bleed, and glass cuts both if left long enough.

**Passerby:** You make the street sound like a scripture.

**Collector:** It is read by those who walk alone.

**Passerby:** Are you alone?

**Collector:** Tonight, yes. But solitude is not emptiness. It is a room where motives can speak plainly.

**Passerby:** And what do yours say?

**Collector:** That no one should inherit harm merely because they arrived after joy.

**Passerby:** Strange. I thought you were collecting bottles.

**Collector:** I am. But every empty thing asks what it once contained—and what it may yet prevent.

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a surreal literary vignette in dialogue form about a “bottle gatherer” taking discarded bottles to a bottle bank shaped like a giant snake head, with dark humor and moral reflection.
counterfactuals.output:
“Do you hear it hissing?” said Mara.

“It’s full of glass,” said the bottle gatherer. “Everything full of glass hisses, if the wind has a talent.”

They stood at the edge of the municipal lot where the bottle bank had been installed: a giant snake head, green-scaled, open-mouthed, with yellow eyes painted in a kind of civic madness. Its tongue was a metal ramp. Its fangs were two chipped concrete posts. Above its mouth, a sign read:

**FEED ME ONLY CLEAN GLASS.  
NO MIRRORS. NO CERAMICS. NO SOULS.**

Mara hugged her coat tight. “That last part is new.”

“They added it after the mayor,” said the bottle gatherer.

“What happened to the mayor?”

“He climbed in to prove it was safe. Came out very clean.”

The bottle gatherer pushed his pram forward. It was heaped with bottles: wine bottles with dry purple throats, beer bottles sticky with old songs, medicine bottles the color of bad advice. They chimed together as he walked, a small, guilty orchestra.

Mara peered into the snake’s mouth. “Why do you do it?”

“Gather bottles?”

“Yes.”

“Because people leave them behind.”

“That’s not a reason.”

“It is the only reason most jobs have.”

The snake head shuddered as the first bottle slid down its tongue. Somewhere inside, glass broke with a bright little scream.

Mara winced. “Doesn’t that bother you?”

“Not as much as when they stay whole.”

He lifted another bottle. Inside it, a tiny paper ship turned slowly in dust.

“Who threw that away?” Mara asked.

“Someone finished the voyage.”

He tossed it in. Crash.

The snake’s painted eyes seemed to moisten.

Mara said, “My mother said men like you are scavengers.”

“My mother said children like you should not talk to men like me.”

“Was she right?”

“Usually mothers are right in ways that don’t help.”

The bottle gatherer pulled out a blue bottle, narrow-necked and elegant. “This one held perfume. Cost more than my winter.”

“What did it smell like?”

“Like a rich woman pretending flowers forgive her.”

He fed it to the snake.

Crash.

A laugh came from deep inside the bank—or perhaps it was only bottles settling into sharper arrangements.

Mara took a step back. “I don’t like that it sounds hungry.”

“It is hungry,” said the bottle gatherer. “But less hungry than us.”

“For bottles?”

“For second chances.”

He reached into the pram again. His hand emerged holding a small brown bottle with a label half-torn away: **TONIC FOR COURAGE**.

Mara read it and frowned. “Did it work?”

“For about twenty minutes, then the man who drank it proposed to a lamppost and fought a mailbox.”

“Did he win?”

“The mailbox had the moral advantage.”

The bottle gatherer turned the bottle in his fingers. “Still, he left it under a bench instead of in the river. Even disgrace can be sorted properly.”

Mara watched him drop it into the snake’s mouth.

Crash.

“Is recycling good?” she asked.

The bottle gatherer sighed. “Good is a large coat. We small people disappear inside it.”

“That sounds like something someone says when they’ve done something bad.”

“It is also what someone says when they has done something good and suspects it is not enough.”

The snake bank groaned. A few green shards glittered on its lip like teeth growing in.

Mara pointed at the sign. “No souls. Do people try?”

“Constantly.”

“Why?”

“They want to be emptied and made useful again.”

“And can they?”

The bottle gatherer looked into the dark throat of the serpent. “Not here.”

A wind crossed the lot, lifting crisp packets and dead leaves. For a moment they moved together in a little procession, as if heading somewhere more dignified.

Mara said, “What happens to the bottles after?”

“They are crushed. Melted. Made into new bottles.”

“So they come back?”

“Yes.”

“That’s horrible.”

“It is also hope.”

She considered this. “To be broken first?”

“Usually.”

The bottle gatherer picked up the last bottle from the pram. It was clear glass, but clouded from within, as if it had once held fog. There was no label.

“What was in that one?” Mara asked.

“My apology.”

“To whom?”

He smiled without amusement. “It never said.”

He held it a moment longer than the others. The snake’s mouth waited, patient and municipal, a public monster with official approval.

Mara whispered, “You don’t have to.”

“That’s the trouble with apologies,” he said. “You can keep them forever and call it dignity.”

Then he let the bottle roll down the metal tongue.

It did not crash.

Instead, from inside the snake came a soft cough, like an old man embarrassed by his own funeral. The bottle gatherer and Mara stood very still.

The snake’s yellow eyes flickered.

A voice from within said, “Unacceptable item.”

Mara grabbed the bottle gatherer’s sleeve. “It talked.”

“Public services are improving.”

The clear bottle rolled back out, whole, and stopped at his boot.

Mara looked up at him. “What now?”

The bottle gatherer bent slowly and picked it up. In the clouded glass, his face wavered—longer, older, more breakable.

“Now,” he said, “I carry it.”

“For how long?”

“Until I find the person it belongs to.”

“What if they’re dead?”

“Then I’ll have to become better without being forgiven.”

Mara kicked a pebble into the snake’s mouth. It vanished without a sound.

“That seems unfair,” she said.

“Yes,” said the bottle gatherer. He placed the rejected bottle carefully back into the empty pram. “But fairness is not the same as cleanliness.”

The snake head loomed above them, stuffed with the town’s transparent sins, waiting to grind them into future vessels.

Mara said, “Will you come back tomorrow?”

“With more bottles.”

“And the apology?”

“With that too.”

Together they turned from the serpent and began down the road. Behind them, the bottle bank gave a satisfied belch, and somewhere in its belly a thousand bottles settled into glittering fragments, each one preparing, against all reason, to be whole again.

“Good sir, why gleanest thou the bottles others drain and cast away?”

The collector smiled, his sack a-glimmer in the dusk.

“Because, dear heart, an empty vessel is not a useless thing. It hath already known laughter, thirst, and parting. I gather not the glass alone, but proof that all which is spent may yet be made to serve.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a two-person dialogue set in a city after nightlife has ended, involving empty wine bottles, recycling, mass shootings, belief in God, and the idea that some journeys must be taken alone.
counterfactuals.output:
**Mara:** The city always looks embarrassed at this hour.

**Jonah:** Embarrassed?

**Mara:** Like it got caught being itself. Neon off. Floors sticky. Everyone gone home pretending they didn’t say what they said.

**Jonah:** Except us.

**Mara:** Except us, dragging a sack of empty wine bottles down Grand Avenue at four in the morning.

**Jonah:** It’s community-minded.

**Mara:** It’s pathetic.

**Jonah:** Recycling is never pathetic.

**Mara:** You sound like a poster in a kindergarten hallway.

**Jonah:** Those posters were right. “Do your part.” “Be kind.” “Don’t run with scissors.”

**Mara:** “Duck and cover.”

**Jonah:** Different hallway.

**Mara:** Same country.

**Jonah:** Yeah.

**Mara:** Sorry.

**Jonah:** Don’t be. It’s hard not to think about it.

**Mara:** The shooting?

**Jonah:** Which one?

**Mara:** Exactly.

**Jonah:** I saw the news on the bar TV while you were talking to that woman in the silver coat.

**Mara:** I wasn’t talking. She was crying.

**Jonah:** Everyone cries in silver coats eventually.

**Mara:** She said her brother won’t go to concerts anymore. Or grocery stores after eight. Or movie theaters if he can’t sit by the exit.

**Jonah:** That’s not irrational.

**Mara:** No. That’s what scares me.

**Jonah:** The bottles are clinking too loud.

**Mara:** Let them. Maybe they’ll scare off the rats.

**Jonah:** Rats aren’t afraid of consequences.

**Mara:** Neither are men with guns.

**Jonah:** Mara.

**Mara:** What? You want me to call them “troubled individuals”? “Lone wolves”? “A tragedy”? We have so many polite words for horror we should recycle those too.

**Jonah:** I don’t know what I want you to say.

**Mara:** I don’t either.

**Jonah:** There’s the bin.

**Mara:** Finally.

**Jonah:** Green glass first?

**Mara:** There’s no first. You throw it in and it breaks.

**Jonah:** Not always.

**Mara:** Jonah.

**Jonah:** What?

**Mara:** You’re sorting grief by color.

**Jonah:** Maybe I am.

**Mara:** Does it help?

**Jonah:** No. But it gives my hands something to do.

**Mara:** Fair.

**Jonah:** Hand me that bottle.

**Mara:** The one with lipstick on it?

**Jonah:** Sure.

**Mara:** Not mine.

**Jonah:** I know.

**Mara:** You don’t have to say it like that.

**Jonah:** Like what?

**Mara:** Like you’re already forgiving me for things I haven’t confessed.

**Jonah:** I’m tired.

**Mara:** Me too.

**Jonah:** Do you still believe in God?

**Mara:** That’s a stupid question to ask beside a recycling bin.

**Jonah:** Maybe it’s the only place to ask it. All the evidence piled up. All the empties.

**Mara:** Evidence of what? That people drink too much? That Saturday turns into Sunday whether you want it to or not?

**Jonah:** That we keep trying to make something clean out of what’s been used.

**Mara:** That’s not God. That’s municipal policy.

**Jonah:** You used to believe.

**Mara:** I used to believe in a lot of things. Safe classrooms. Wedding vows. The idea that if you screamed, someone would come.

**Jonah:** Someone usually does.

**Mara:** Usually is a terrible word.

**Jonah:** Yeah.

**Mara:** Do you?

**Jonah:** Believe in God?

**Mara:** No, believe these bottles are going to reincarnate as artisan vases.

**Jonah:** I don’t know.

**Mara:** About the vases?

**Jonah:** About God.

**Mara:** That’s honest.

**Jonah:** Some nights I do. Some nights I think belief is just a candle people carry because the dark doesn’t care whether you can see.

**Mara:** That’s almost beautiful.

**Jonah:** Almost?

**Mara:** Don’t get proud.

**Jonah:** Never.

**Mara:** I think I believe in God when someone does something kind and useless.

**Jonah:** Useless?

**Mara:** Not strategic. Not profitable. Like holding a stranger’s hair back in an alley. Like walking six blocks to recycle bottles when we could’ve left them by the curb.

**Jonah:** That might just be guilt.

**Mara:** Maybe God and guilt share an office.

**Jonah:** With bad fluorescent lighting.

**Mara:** And a receptionist who judges your shoes.

**Jonah:** I’d go there.

**Mara:** You go everywhere.

**Jonah:** Not everywhere.

**Mara:** You wanted to come with me tomorrow.

**Jonah:** I still do.

**Mara:** I know.

**Jonah:** Then let me.

**Mara:** No.

**Jonah:** It’s a long bus ride.

**Mara:** I can read.

**Jonah:** It’s your mother’s house.

**Mara:** I know where it is.

**Jonah:** It’s his town too.

**Mara:** Don’t say “his” like he’s a weather system.

**Jonah:** Your husband’s town.

**Mara:** Ex-husband.

**Jonah:** Not yet.

**Mara:** In every way that matters.

**Jonah:** Mara—

**Mara:** Some journeys have to be taken alone.

**Jonah:** People say that when they’re trying to keep others out.

**Mara:** Sometimes people need to be kept out.

**Jonah:** I’m not trying to fix you.

**Mara:** Everyone says that right before they unpack their toolbox.

**Jonah:** I just don’t want you standing in that driveway by yourself.

**Mara:** That’s exactly why I have to.

**Jonah:** Because you’re stubborn?

**Mara:** Because I left by myself in the middle of the night with one bag and no shoes, and I need to go back by myself in daylight and get the rest of my life.

**Jonah:** I could wait at the station.

**Mara:** No.

**Jonah:** Across the street?

**Mara:** Jonah.

**Jonah:** In spirit?

**Mara:** Fine. Haunt me from a respectful distance.

**Jonah:** I can do that.

**Mara:** I know you can.

**Jonah:** Another bottle.

**Mara:** Last one.

**Jonah:** It didn’t break.

**Mara:** See? Miracles.

**Jonah:** Municipal miracles.

**Mara:** Maybe that’s all we get.

**Jonah:** Maybe that’s enough.

**Mara:** Is it?

**Jonah:** Tonight? No.

**Mara:** Good answer.

**Jonah:** Tomorrow, when you’re on the bus, will you text me when you get there?

**Mara:** Yes.

**Jonah:** And when you leave?

**Mara:** Yes.

**Jonah:** And if you get scared?

**Mara:** Especially then.

**Jonah:** That doesn’t sound alone.

**Mara:** Alone doesn’t mean unloved.

**Jonah:** No?

**Mara:** No. It means no one else can take the steps for you.

**Jonah:** I hate that.

**Mara:** Everyone does.

**Jonah:** The sun’s coming up.

**Mara:** Poor thing. It has to look at all this again.

**Jonah:** Maybe it believes in us.

**Mara:** Now who believes in God?

**Jonah:** I said maybe.

**Mara:** Come on. Let’s get coffee before the city remembers what it is.

**Jonah:** Mara?

**Mara:** Yeah?

**Jonah:** For what it’s worth, I’ll be here when you get back.

**Mara:** I know.

**Jonah:** You do?

**Mara:** That’s why I can go.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a strange modern parable made entirely of dialogue, featuring a bottle collector, a curious stranger, references to bottle colors as a metaphor for race, and a closing line about solitude.
counterfactuals.output:
“Why do you pull bottles from the river at dawn?”

“Because the river forgets what the city throws away.”

“And you remember for it?”

“I sort what floats back.”

“By shape?”

“By color.”

“That seems dangerous.”

“Only if you believe color is the bottle.”

“What else could it be?”

“A coat of light. A rumor from sand. A mistake the furnace made beautiful.”

“You have green ones here.”

“Green bottles think they were born from forests.”

“And brown ones?”

“Brown bottles survive sunlight better than most. They keep what is inside from spoiling.”

“And the clear ones?”

“They are praised for showing everything, though they break like the rest.”

“What about the blue bottle on the highest shelf?”

“That one was called rare until the others grew tired of hearing it.”

“Do they argue?”

“At night.”

“About what?”

“Who held wine, who held poison, who was touched by clean hands, who was stepped over in the street.”

“That sounds like people.”

“People learned it from bottles.”

“No, bottles learned it from people.”

“Then both have been badly taught.”

“Why not melt them down together?”

“I tried once.”

“What happened?”

“They became a single dark glass, and everyone who looked into it saw their own face.”

“Was that not good?”

“They called it impure.”

“Who did?”

“The ones who preferred shelves.”

“And you?”

“I prefer windows.”

“Then why keep them separated?”

“So visitors like you will ask the question.”

“And what answer am I supposed to find?”

“That a bottle’s color may tell you what it endured, but never what it can carry.”

“What can they carry now?”

“Rainwater. Fireflies. Apologies. Small gods with nowhere else to sleep.”

“May I take one?”

“Only if you promise not to call it empty.”

“I promise.”

“Choose.”

“I’ll take the cracked brown one.”

“Why?”

“Because the light inside it looks patient.”

“Then go carefully.”

“Will you be here tomorrow?”

“If the river returns anything.”

“And if it does not?”

“Then I will sit among the bottles and listen to the loud shape of solitude.”
